author: Ajeya Krishna
text:
Your LLM gateway adds 0.66 ms of latency.
Your LLM call takes 812 ms.
Stop worrying about the gateway.

Most teams I talk to skip an AI gateway for one reason:
"It's another hop. It'll slow us down."

The numbers say otherwise.

LiteLLM's new Rust gateway benchmarks at:
→ 0.66 ms added latency (p99)
→ ~22 MB memory at rest
→ 2,800+ requests/sec at ~21% CPU

That's ~0.08% of a typical LLM call.

Meanwhile, here's what that 0.66 ms buys you on every single request:

1. Virtual keys: no raw provider keys in your apps
2. Rate limits: TPM/RPM per team or model
3. Hard budgets: at the cap, requests stop
4. Guardrails: PII masking and prompt-injection checks
5. Semantic caching: repeat prompts cost $0
6. Smart routing: cheap models for easy prompts, strong ones for hard prompts
7. Auto fallback: OpenAI returns 429, Claude answers instead
8. Full tracing: every request, every dollar, every team

And your code?
Still the OpenAI SDK. You only change the base_url.

The GIF shows one request going through all 8 steps, including a live fallback and a cache hit.

The real question isn't "will a gateway slow us down?"
It's "can we afford to run LLMs in production without one?"

Are you calling LLM providers directly, or through a gateway?

comments.author: Commenter A
comments.text: In our setup the gateway was never the slow part; the model call was. What mattered was stopping a team at its budget and keeping fallback responses the same shape.

replies.author: Ajeya Krishna
replies.text:
Commenter A For your problem, the right approach would be to thoroughly test every prompt and model you plan to configure as a fallback.

We shouldn't add a model to the fallback chain without first running regression tests against a representative golden dataset. This allows us to compare the fallback model's behavior with the primary model and verify that quality remains within acceptable thresholds.

Along with regression testing, we should have output validation checks in place for correctness, format, safety, and any use-case-specific constraints. This gives us measurable confidence that switching to a fallback model won't unexpectedly degrade the user experience.
